title: India Almost Missed the World Cup. Then Zee Signed an Eight-Year Deal Ten Days Before Kickoff.
excerpt: Zee Entertainment secures FIFA broadcast rights through 2034 for roughly $60 million, ending months of uncertainty and launching the Unite8 Sports network in the process.
body:
Ten days before the biggest FIFA World Cup in history kicks off across North America, Indian football fans can finally exhale. Zee Entertainment Enterprises has secured the broadcast rights for the 2026 tournament — and for every major FIFA event through 2034.

The deal, finalised on June 1, ends what had become an embarrassing saga for one of the world's largest football-watching nations. For months, India had no confirmed broadcaster for a tournament that will feature 48 teams playing 104 matches across the United States, Canada, and Mexico starting June 11. China's state broadcaster CMG sealed its deal with FIFA on May 15. India was still waiting.

## What Happened

The breakdown started with JioStar, the merged entity of India's two largest sports broadcasters. Negotiations between JioStar and FIFA stalled over valuation disagreements. FIFA initially sought close to $100 million for the India broadcast package. JioStar, having just digested the massive integration of Jio Cinema and Star Sports, apparently decided the price was too steep.

That left a vacuum. The Delhi High Court stepped in on May 12, issuing notices to the Centre and Prasar Bharati after a petition sought directions to ensure the World Cup would be broadcast on free-to-air platforms like Doordarshan and DD Sports. An Indian-American firm from Washington, DC — Avni LLC, led by CEO Deelip Mhaske — even emerged as a surprise claimant, saying an associated partner had secured the winning bid in FIFA's closed tender process. FIFA responded only that discussions "are ongoing and must remain confidential."

Then Zee struck. The company signed an eight-year agreement covering 39 FIFA events from 2026 through 2034, including the 2030 World Cup, the 2027 Women's World Cup, and multiple youth and futsal tournaments. The reported price: approximately $60 million, a 40 per cent discount from FIFA's original ask.

## Where to Watch

The World Cup will air on Zee's brand-new Unite8 Sports network, a suite of four linear channels that did not exist until this deal required them. Unite8 Sports 1 and its HD variant will carry Hindi-language coverage. Unite8 Sports 2 and HD will broadcast in English. Zee Bangla Sonar will carry Bengali coverage, and Zee Keralam will handle Malayalam.

All 104 matches will also stream live on ZEE5, Zee's digital platform. That last detail matters enormously for the Indian diaspora. NRIs across North America, the United Kingdom, and the Gulf will be able to stream matches in Hindi and regional languages from their phones — a capability that JioStar's cricket-centric infrastructure would have provided but never got the chance to.

## The Price of Watching

Not everyone is celebrating. ZEE5 is reportedly offering a three-month World Cup package for ₹799 — with advertisements included. The pricing triggered an immediate backlash on social media, with fans pointing out that the tournament itself runs only about five weeks, not three months.

"₹799 is diabolical. Illegal streams FTW," one fan wrote on X. Others questioned whether a basic cable subscription to Unite8 Sports would actually work out cheaper than the digital option.

## What It Means for Zee

For Zee Entertainment, the deal is a strategic re-entry into sports broadcasting roughly eight years after the company sold its previous sports assets to Sony. Shares rose approximately seven per cent on the announcement.

The acquisition is a bet that Indian football viewership is worth owning for the long term. The 2022 World Cup in Qatar drew an estimated 200 million Indian viewers across platforms. With the 2026 edition being held in US and Canadian time zones — overlapping conveniently with Indian late-night and early-morning viewing habits — Zee is banking on even higher numbers, particularly from the diaspora audience.

The eight-year window also gives Zee a lock on the 2030 World Cup, which will be co-hosted by Morocco, Spain, and Portugal, with matches also in Argentina, Paraguay, and Uruguay. That tournament is expected to draw even larger Indian audiences as football's popularity in the country continues to grow.

For now, the immediate crisis is over. India will not be the country that missed the World Cup. But the fact that it came this close — with a high court having to intervene and an unknown DC firm making last-minute claims — says something about the structural chaos that still governs Indian sports broadcasting.

*Sources: The Indian Eye, Khel Now, myKhel, SacNilk, Indulge Express*
